papers.title: The Human Contraceptive Antibody Targets A Semenogelin Galectin-3 N-Linked Glycan Complex on the Sperm Surface
papers.abstract: The human contraception antibody (HCA) is a non-hormonal topical contraceptive entering Phase II clinical trials that functions by agglutinating and immobilizing sperm. To date, the HCA epitope has been described as an N-linked polylactosamine glycan motif on CD52, but this assignment has been inferred only by colocalization with anti-CD52 and S19 antibodies in western blots. Here, we report that HCA may instead bind semenogelin-galectin-3 complexes associated with the sperm surface. Semenogelins are gel forming, highly glycosylated proteins, with molecular weights of 50-70 kDa that are cleaved into smaller segments that adhere to sperm during semen liquefaction. In this study, we isolated the HCA antigen from seminal plasma and sperm using an HCA affinity column and identified semenogelin by mass spectrometry. Western blot analysis of seminal plasma showed that HCA binds to a large smear of proteins with a higher apparent molecular mass than CD52, and that these may correspond to semenogelin sequences. Flow cytometric analysis of enzymatically deglycosylated sperm demonstrated that HCA binding requires sperm surface N-linked glycans. However, despite this apparent glycan dependence, HCA failed to bind any glycans represented on a comprehensive glycan microarray. In addition to semenogelin, Galectin-3 was identified in the HCA purified sperm lysates, supporting a model in which HCA recognizes semenogelin-derived glycopeptides that are tethered to the sperm surface via a galectin mediated interaction with an N-linked glycan. We found that O-linked glycan modifications on the semenogelin proteins contain LacNAc motifs that can bind to galectins. Finally, we found that depletion of galectins bound to the sperm surface by competitive inhibitors reduced HCA-mediated agglutination, and this could be rescued by addition of recombinant galectin-3/semenogelin-2 complexes to sperm cultures. Collectively, our findings suggest that HCA's binding site involves a semenogelin-galectin-3 complex anchored to the sperm surface via an N-linked glycan.

papers.title: Stemness overcomes IFNγ-induced antitumour exhaustion in human macrophages
papers.abstract: Macrophages hold great promise for antitumour therapies (1-4), particularly owing to their ability to infiltrate solid tumours (5). Yet therapeutic success has been limited (6,7), because macrophages exhibit rapid exhaustion of antitumorigenic activity in the tumour (5,8,9). Here, we induced a stem-like self-renewal programme in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived macrophages by deleting the self-renewal restricting transcription factors MAFB and MAF (MAF-DKO). Human MAF-DKO macrophages showed activated stem cell signatures, increased clonogenicity and proliferative potential. Increased self-renewal capacity was accompanied by enhanced mitochondrial fitness and invigorated energy metabolism. Importantly, these stemness features prevented exhaustion, cellular aging-associated parameters and loss of energy efficiency that are typically associated with proinflammatory macrophage activation. In addition, activated MAF-DKO macrophages showed a broad loss of IFN{gamma}-triggered immunosuppressive pathways (10,11), induced a super-activated state with robust cytotoxic activity and resisted exhaustion upon tumour cell exposure. Consequently, activated MAF-DKO macrophages showed intratumoral persistence with a stable antitumoral phenotype in vivo, conferred robust reduction of tumour burden and extended survival of tumour-bearing mice. Together, this demonstrates that the induction of stemness in human macrophages can overcome critical roadblocks of antitumour therapy by conferring resistance to activation-triggered exhaustion of antitumour activity in the TME.

papers.title: NOD2 restrains probiotic-mediated TLR2-dependent antitumor immunity
papers.abstract: The gut microbiota influences cancer immunotherapy, but how interactions among host microbial sensors determine the activity of individual bacteria remains unclear. Here, we show that NOD2 restrains TLR2-dependent antitumor immunity induced by Lactiplantibacillus plantarum. Oral administration of live or heat-killed L. plantarum enhanced immune checkpoint blockade efficacy in mouse tumor models. This activity required host TLR2 signaling and was diminished by disruption of bacterial lipoprotein. In contrast, NOD2 deficiency enhanced tumor control, intratumoral interferon-associated programs, and T cell activation. NOD2 deficiency also amplified chemokine and interferon-associated responses to L. plantarum and the synthetic TLR2 agonist Pam3CSK4 in myeloid cells. Genetic loss or pharmacological inhibition of NOD2 improved Pam3CSK4-mediated tumor control in combination with checkpoint blockade. These findings identify NOD2 as a functional checkpoint on TLR2-driven antitumor immunity and demonstrate that interactions between host microbial-sensing pathways shape the therapeutic activity of commensal bacteria and innate immune agonists.

papers.title: A 21-Color Spectral Flow Cytometry Panel for Comprehensive Immunophenotyping of Rat Tissues and a Companion 9-Color T-Cell Functional Assay
papers.abstract: Although rats are crucial translational research models due to their immunological homology and surgical feasibility, the scarcity of conjugated antibodies has hampered high-dimensional immune profiling. To bridge this gap, we created a synergistic two-panel method that uses full-spectral flow cytometry: a 21-color comprehensive immunophenotyping panel and a 9-color intracellular cytokine staining (ICS) panel. The 21-color panel navigates the limited fluorophore pool and maps innate and adaptive lineages at high resolution. While it can be used to profile neutrophils and monocytes in peripheral blood it reaches its full potential in lymphoid organs, allowing for the simultaneous evaluation of tissue-resident macrophages, dendritic cells, T cell differentiation (including Tregs), and APC function. Based on this phenotypic paradigm, the 9-color ICS panel dissects effector T cell activation and Th1/Th2/Th17 cytokine production. Furthermore, we reserved the PE color during panel creation, allowing for the use of antibodies and probes with PE or comparable fluorophores in conjunction with this panel, hence increasing overall flexibility. This combination technique, designed for rat peripheral blood, spleen, and lymph nodes, combines panoramic phenotyping with functional analysis, offering an adaptable foundation for complicated tissue microenvironments in tumor immunology, rheumatology, and autoimmunity research.

papers.title: Self-reactive human CD8⁺ T cells restricted by HLA-E mediate immunoregulatory and antiviral functions
papers.abstract: HLA-E constitutively presents self VL9 peptides on healthy cells, signaling an intact HLA class I pathway and protecting cells from natural killer cell attack. Beyond this canonical role, HLA-E-restricted CD8 T cells that recognize foreign pathogen peptides have emerged as mediators of immunity in multiple human infections, with orthologous responses conferring unprecedented protection in an HIV vaccine model. However, the poor stability of most pathogen-derived HLA-E ligands raises the possibility that additional modes of HLA-E-restricted recognition remain undiscovered. Here, we establish an alternative paradigm in which HLA-E-restricted CD8+ T cells recognize disease-associated increases in self-VL9/HLA-E rather than foreign antigen. These cells, which we term E-sensors, integrate activating and inhibitory signals to discriminate physiological from pathological levels of HLA-E expression. We demonstrate that E-sensors selectively eliminate highly activated, proliferating immune cells that express high levels of HLA-E, establishing a mechanistically resolved pathway of human CD8+ T cell immunoregulation. E-sensors also recognize pathogen-induced HLA-E upregulation and directly eliminate infected cells without prior pathogen-specific priming, demonstrating immediate immunosurveillance through recognition of increased self. Consistent with this antiviral function, we establish E-sensors as a previously unrecognized component of spontaneous HIV immune control in persons who naturally control infection. Together, our findings establish a pathway of human immunosurveillance and immunoregulation in which CD8 T cells detect pathological increases in a constitutively expressed non-classical HLA class I molecule presenting a conserved self-peptide. This disease-agnostic mechanism of immune recognition has implications across infection, cancer, autoimmune disease, and other pathologies that upregulate HLA-E. Unlike classical HLA class I molecules, the near-monomorphic nature of HLA-E further positions this pathway as an untapped effector axis, warranting investigation as a potential target for immune interventions.

papers.title: Dual-Antigen CCHFV Vaccine Induces Neutralizing Immunity and Protection Against Lethal Challenge
papers.abstract: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is a WHO-priority pathogen with high mortality and wide global distribution. A major challenge in CCHFV vaccine development is identifying antigens that induce functional cellular and humoral immunity. We previously showed that the CCHF nucleoprotein (NP) elicits protective responses in mice and non-human primates but does not induce neutralizing antibodies. We therefore systematically screened six chimeric DNA vaccines expressing different CCHF glycoproteins combined with NP. A construct comprising the ectodomain of the glycoprotein Gc and NP elicited robust antibody and T-cell responses to both antigens. The Gc-NP gene was subsequently developed as a lipid nanoparticle-formulated mRNA vaccine using a scalable manufacturing pipeline. Gc-NP mRNA-LNP induced robust antigen-specific humoral and cellular responses comparable to those elicited by the corresponding DNA vaccine, despite the substantially lower dose. Both vaccine approaches generated Gc-directed neutralizing antibody responses against CCHFV pseudovirus and protected mice against homologous Hoti and heterologous IbAr10200 strain challenge. These findings demonstrate that systematic antigen screening combined with genetic vaccine platforms can identify a potent multi-antigen CCHF vaccine candidate.

papers.title: Human caspase-4 and caspase-5 assemble into non-canonical inflammasomes in response to overlapping and distinct LPS structures
papers.abstract: Innate immune sensing of bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is critical to host defense, but a dysregulated response can lead to sepsis, a life-threatening condition associated with multiple organ failure and shock. LPS is sensed at the cell surface by Toll-Like Receptor 4 (TLR4) and in the cytosol by mouse caspase-11 (Casp11) or its human orthologs, caspase-4 and 5 (CASP4/5). In response to cytosolic LPS, Casp11 oligomerizes in a catalytically dependent manner into supramolecular organizing centers (SMOCs). We demonstrate that CASP4 and CASP5 also form catalytically dependent SMOCs in response to bacterial LPS in macrophages. Furthermore, we find that CASP4 and CASP5 differentially respond to distinct LPS structural variants that fail to activate CASP11 and that only activating LPS structures induce SMOC formation by the corresponding caspase. Notably, transgenic mice expressing CASP4 in lieu of Casp11 exert more effective control of Francisella novicida, a rodent pathogen whose LPS evades TLR4 and Casp11 detection. Conversely, CASP4-expressing mice are more susceptible to sepsis when exposed to E. coli expressing a lipid A variant that fails to activate TLR4 and Casp11. Together, these findings reveal human CASP4 and CASP5 have evolved to assemble into SMOCs in response to a broader range of LPS structures than mouse Casp11 and highlight the potential tradeoff between systemic inflammation and control of bacterial infection that may underline these differences. Our findings may inform the development of targeted therapeutic strategies for gram-negative bacterial infection and sepsis that are effective in humans.

papers.title: In vitro-generated murine monocyte-derived dendritic cells habor a unique identity compared to other mononuclear phagocytes, largely conserved with their human and putative in vivo counterparts.
papers.abstract: Whether the cells differentiating in vitro from total murine bone marrow (BM) cultures with GM-CSF +/- IL-4 are homologous to the human cells derived in vitro from purified circulating monocytes (Mo) cultured with GM-CSF and IL-4, mostly correspond to monocyte-derived dendritic cells (moDCs) or rather to macrophages (MFs), and have in vivo counterparts, is debated. It has been proposed to define cell types based on their ontogeny, leading to the proposal of excluding from the dendritic cell (DC) family the cells that do not arise from the common DC progenitors (CDP). However, recent discoveries support defining cell types rather by functions, or, as a surrogate, their instructive molecular networks. Indeed, Langerhans cells, Rorgt+ DCs, some cDC2As and human in vitro-derived moDCs do not arise from the CDP but exert hallmark DC functions instructed by specific transcriptomic modules shared with cDCs. Actually, the study of both LCs and moDCs has been key for dissecting DC biology. Yet, the existence of moDCs is put into questions. The functions once attributed to moDCs are now proposed to be exerted by type 2B conventional DCs (cDC2Bs) or type 3 DCs (DC3s) that have been characterized recently, harbor strongly overlapping phenotypes with moDCs and a similar mixed expression of genes from both the cDC and Mo/MF lineages, but a different ontogeny. To clarify these issues, we generated a transcriptomic atlas of in vitro-derived mononuclear phagocytes (MNPs). We show that moDCs are the only DC type arising in BM cultures in the presence of GM-CSF and IL-4. They express a unique transcriptomic and phenotypic signature, different from those of cDC2Bs and DC3s that are produced in FLT3-L cultures and appear to correspond to the same DC type differentiating though two different but converging ontogenetic paths. By harnessing the phenotypic and transcriptomic signatures identified from the analysis of our in vitro MNP atlas, we are able to identify in vivo a population of putative DCs differentiated from monocytes derived from the common monocyte-granulocyte progenitor (GMP), in a respiratory allergy model, specifically in the lungs of mice sensitized to house dust mite (HDM). Using the model of thioglycolate-induced peritonitis, we also characterized the CD226+ Mo-derived cells that have been reported to be moDCs or small cavity MFs (SCM) depending on studies. We showed that these cells are mainly differentiated from monocytes derived from the MDP, and split into two populations, one resembling MFs (SCMs) and the other one closer to lung moDCs but expressing distinct genes suggesting a different functional potential. Collectively, we show that the generation and characterization of specific MNP types in vitro can be harnessed to rigorously define their in vivo counterparts based on phenotypic analysis and gene module assessment, as we demonstrate for moDCs.

papers.title: Fever-range temperature enhances B cells in vitro but is dispensable for the germinal center in vivo
papers.abstract: Fever is a conserved physiological response to immune activation characterized by elevated body temperature. While hyperthermia enhances innate and T cell immunity, its role in shaping the B cell compartment remains poorly defined, despite B cells' role in long-term protection. Understanding how temperature modulates B cell physiology is relevant to vaccine strategies, particularly fever management around immunization. Therefore, we investigated the influence of fever-range thermal changes on humoral immunity. To decipher the direct effects, primary B cells from C57BL/6 mice were stimulated in vitro under mild hyperthermic conditions (~1.5{degrees}C increase). Fever-range temperature enhanced B cell activation, facilitated entry into cell division, and increased antigen presentation to CD4+ T cells, while transcriptomic analysis revealed enrichment of pathways involved in protein synthesis and mitochondrial respiration. To determine whether these intrinsic effects translated into altered humoral immunity in vivo, we developed a novel tunable implant-based system to induce localized, 48-hour hyperthermia around a draining lymph node in awake mice without altering core body temperature. Following subcutaneous NP-OVA/alum immunization, localized hyperthermia localized hyperthermia did not enhance antigen-specific germinal center B cell expansion, antibody titers or IgG affinity on day 9. Moreover, heating during priming did not affect the recall humoral response after a booster on day 21. Thus, fever-range temperature directly modulates murine B cell function in vitro but does not enhance humoral immunity in vivo, indicating that the biological consequences of intrinsic B cell thermosensitivity depend on its integration within the multicellular and inflammatory signals shaping germinal center responses.

papers.title: Anti-inflammatory macrophages limit endothelial inflammation and restrict neutrophil recruitment through Gas6/AXL signaling
papers.abstract: Neutrophil extravasation requires coordinated interactions between the endothelium and surrounding cells, including tissue resident macrophages. Macrophages adopt distinct polarization states in the tissue environment, positioning them as regulators of vascular inflammation. However, how these states influence barrier function and neutrophil extravasation remains unclear. Here, we polarized macrophages in the matrix surrounding an endothelial vessel, in a three-dimensional inflammation-on-a-chip model developed only from primary human cells. We found anti-inflammatory macrophages limited endothelial inflammation, reducing ICAM-1 upregulation, maintaining VE-Cadherin expression, halving permeability relative to pro-inflammatory devices, and reducing neutrophil extravasation and migration relative to macrophage-free devices. Secretome profiling identified Gas6, an AXL ligand, as a potential regulator of these effects. Inhibiting AXL increased extravasation in devices with anti-inflammatory macrophages, and soluble Gas6 reduced extravasation in macrophage-free devices, implicating Gas6 as a mediator of this regulation. This indicates macrophages regulate endothelial inflammation and the neutrophil response via Gas6 signaling.

papers.title: Apoptotic Cells Promote Tim4+ Macrophage Differentiation Through Direct and Indirect Signaling Pathways
papers.abstract: Tissue macrophages are the primary cells responsible for efficiently clearing apoptotic cells, yet how professional efferocyte populations are established remains unclear. Tim4 marks a subset of macrophages across multiple tissues that are highly efferocytic, but the mechanisms governing Tim4 acquisition are poorly understood. Here, we show that monocyte-derived macrophages progressively differentiate into Tim4 macrophages in homeostatic and pathological settings. We identify a cell-autonomous pathway in which efficient apoptotic cell clearance promotes Tim4 acquisition in macrophages, as combined deficiency of CD11b and MerTK impairs both efferocytosis and Tim4 acquisition. Surprisingly, excessive apoptotic cell burden enhanced Tim4 acquisition independently of these receptors. We demonstrate that serial exposure to apoptotic cells induces a type 2 immune response characterized by expansion of IL-4-producing populations and that IL-4R-STAT6 signaling is sufficient and required to drive Tim4 acquisition. These findings support a model in which Tim4 acquisition in macrophages integrates direct signals associated with apoptotic cell clearance and indirect signals generated by apoptotic cell burden. We propose that these complementary mechanisms enable tissues to dynamically adjust the size and function of the professional efferocyte compartment to meet changing demands for apoptotic cell clearance.

papers.title: Diacylglycerol Kinases Balance DAG Signaling to Control B Cell Maturation, Germinal Center Homeostasis, and Humoral Immunity
papers.abstract: Diacylglycerol (DAG) is a critical second messenger downstream of the B-cell receptor (BCR), but how DAG signaling is regulated during B-cell development and humoral responses remains incompletely understood. Here, complementary gain- and loss-of-function approaches revealed stage-specific requirements for diacylglycerol kinase (DGK)-regulated signaling in B cells. Expression of the gain-of-function DGK{zeta} mutant DGK{zeta}{Delta}NLS had limited effects on early BM B-cell development but progressively impaired transitional and mature B-cell populations. DGK{zeta}{Delta}NLS attenuated BCR-induced ERK1/2 and mTOR signaling, activation, and proliferation and, when expressed in AID-expressing B cells, reduced GC B-cell survival and T-dependent IgG responses without detectably impairing GC B-cell proliferation in vivo. Conversely, combined DGK/{zeta} deficiency resulted in marked spontaneous GC B-cell expansion associated with enhanced ERK1/2, Akt, and S6 signaling and increased glucose uptake. Despite this steady-state GC expansion, DGK/{zeta}-deficient mice developed spontaneous autoreactivity and mounted impaired antigen-specific antibody responses. Thus, B-cell developmental stages exhibit differential sensitivity to altered DGK activity, and opposing perturbations of DGK-regulated signaling produce reciprocal effects on GC B-cell accumulation while both compromise productive humoral immunity. These findings identify DGKs as critical regulators that tune lipid signaling for B-cell maturation, GC homeostasis, and effective antibody responses.

papers.title: TLR7-Dependent Autoimmunity Remodels Intestinal Immune Cell Dissemination
papers.abstract: Intestinal immune cell dissemination has emerged as a fundamental mechanism of tissue-to-tissue immune communication that shapes systemic immunity, yet how this physiological process changes across different stages of systemic autoimmunity remains poorly understood. Here, using photoconversion, inducible and spontaneous models of TLR7-dependent autoimmunity, and microbiota perturbation, we define how autoimmunity reshapes intestinal immune dissemination. TLR7-dependent autoimmunity progressively suppresses dissemination in a tissue-dependent manner across gut-associated and systemic tissues while selectively reconfiguring the intestinal emigrant pool, characterized by reduced lymphocyte dissemination and increased representation of myeloid populations, particularly dendritic cells. This divergence is already evident in young TLR7-transgenic mice before detectable splenomegaly. Moreover, microbial regulation of intestinal dissemination depends on timing and inflammatory context, with antibiotic treatment during ongoing autoimmunity producing broader changes in intestinal immune dissemination. Together, our findings establish remodeling of physiological intestinal immune dissemination as an early feature of TLR7-dependent autoimmunity and reveal how chronic inflammation reshapes tissue-to-tissue immune communication.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal profiling of T cell repertoires in Lynch syndrome reveals convergent immune responses through neoplastic progression
papers.abstract: Surveillance of individuals with Lynch syndrome (LS), who are carriers of heterozygous inactivating mismatch repair (MMR) gene mutations that predispose to colorectal cancer, enables the study of tumour-immune coevolution during tumour initiation. Somatic loss of MMR activity in the LS colon leads to the accrual of cancer driver mutations, and also of neoantigens likely to generate an adaptive immune response. However, the spatial and temporal immune dynamics in colon and peripheral blood are uncharacterised. Here we show that the neoplastic evolution of mismatch repair deficient (MMRd) clones leads to large-scale and sustained reorganisation of the T-cell repertoire in colon and peripheral blood. We performed dense spatiotemporal profiling of T cell receptor (TCR) repertoires from 109 colonic biopsies (11 tumour samples, 98 normal bowel) from seven individuals, with eight matched blood repertoires. We additionally analysed 13 colorectal polyp repertoires from eight participants, 286 cross sectional blood repertoires from 242 participants (198 LS and 44 non-LS) and 52 longitudinal peripheral blood samples from 26 individuals with LS. We detected tumour-associated T cell clones, some of which were widely present in normal bowel tissue and also detectable in peripheral blood. Sequence similarity analysis revealed conserved TCR architectures across tissue compartments and recurrent clustering patterns between patients, that were not present in non-Lynch controls, consistent with convergent MMRd-associated antigen-driven immune selection. We identified systemic signatures associated with local tumour immune activity and revealed evidence of structured repertoire remodelling before overt malignancy. Longitudinal profiling revealed frequent turnover of low-abundance clonotypes, whereas highly abundant clonotypes persisted for several years. Collectively, our data defines the local and circulating TCR landscape associated with colonic neoplasia in LS, and provides a framework for LS blood-based immune monitoring, early interception and biomarker development.

papers.title: T cell engagers convert acute tumor killing into endogenous vaccination
papers.abstract: T cell engagers (TCEs) redirect T cells to kill tumors by cross-linking CD3{varepsilon} to a tumor antigen, independently of T cell receptor specificity. Some patients achieve remissions that persist long after drug clearance, but whether TCEs can couple acute cytotoxicity to the generation of lasting adaptive immunity remains unknown. Here, using an immunocompetent mouse model for clinical-grade human TCEs, we show that TCE-mediated killing initiates an endogenous vaccination cascade. Intravital two-photon imaging reveals a perforin-dependent cytotoxic wave that peaks within 24 hours, then subsides despite massive T cell accumulation. Single-cell transcriptomics and adoptive transfers demonstrate that memory CD8 T cells, the principal effector reservoir in mouse and human, transit through a progenitor-like state before differentiating into cytotoxic effectors with recall competence. Crucially, tumor lysis fuels cross-priming of tumor-specific CD8 T cells by XCR1 type 1 conventional dendritic cells, a cDC1-dependent step essential for durable tumor control and protective memory upon rechallenge.

papers.title: A monoallelic immunopeptidome atlas of 10 prevalent canine DLA-88 alleles
papers.abstract: Characterization of naturally processed MHC class I (MHC-I)-bound peptides is essential for defining allele-specific peptide-binding features and understanding the functional consequences of MHC-I polymorphism. However, immunopeptidome analyses of dog leukocyte antigen (DLA) class I (DLA-I) molecules remain limited and comprehensive monoallelic ligand datasets for prevalent DLA-88 alleles are still lacking. Here, we established canine melanoma-derived cell populations expressing individual functional DLA-88 alleles and generated a monoallelic immunopeptidome atlas of prevalent DLA-88 alleles. Using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, we identified 32,702 naturally processed peptides of 7 to15 amino acids across 10 DLA-88 alleles, substantially expanding the available DLA-88 immunopeptidome landscape. These 10 alleles exhibited canonical peptide length distributions and allele-specific binding motifs that reflected variation in binding-groove pseudo-sequences defined from human MHC-I peptide-contact residues. Ligand sharing between DLA-88 alleles was associated with binding site distance. Incorporation of the comprehensively characterized DLA-88 ligand datasets in this study increased by more than fourfold the number of published canine DLA-I alleles with ligand-characterized reference alleles predicted to have similar peptide-binding features. We also found that antigen-processing signatures were highly conserved with those reported in humans. As a proof-of-concept application, we selected 54 DLA-88-bound peptides identified in our immunopeptidome analysis as candidate peptides for canine cancer immunotherapy by evaluating the normal tissue expression profiles of their source proteins. This DLA-88 immunopeptidome atlas provides insights into allele-dependent differences in antigen presentation and represents a valuable resource for developing accurate DLA-88-binding peptide prediction tools and supporting peptide-based immunological studies in dogs.

papers.title: T-bet marks contact-capable regulatory T cells embedded within Th1-dendritic cell networks in skin-draining lymph nodes
papers.abstract: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) adapt to inflammatory environments while preserving Foxp3-dependent suppressive identity. In type 1 inflammation, Tregs can upregulate T-bet, but whether T-bet Tregs represent a stable regulatory subset or exhibit plasticity toward an effector-like state remains incompletely understood. To probe the positioning and interactions of T-bet Tregs during type 1 inflammation, we performed live lymph node section microscopy in T-bet-ZsGreen Foxp3-RFP dual-reporter mice during a subcutaneous complete Freunds adjuvant (CFA) challenge. T-bet Tregs accumulated rapidly in the draining lymph nodes within 24 hours, coincident with the appearance of T-bet dendritic cells (DCs) and Th1-like CD4 T cells. Analysis of lymph node sections revealed that T-bet Tregs were incorporated into Th1-DC contact networks, displaying increased contact frequency and contact volume compared with T-bet- Tregs. In parallel, flow cytometric analysis of the immune response showed that T-bet Tregs maintained a stable regulatory profile distinct from T-bet effector T cells, with retained high expression of Foxp3 and regulatory-associated surface molecules including FR4, CD25, Nrp-1, CD39, and GARP. They also expressed elevated adhesion and activation-associated molecules, including LFA-1, ICOS, PD-1, CD44, and CD103 compared with T-bet- Tregs, and were enriched for CD103 cells across the inflammatory time course. Adoptive transfer studies further showed that pre-existing T-bet expression enhanced recovery of antigen-specific Tregs from CFA-draining lymph nodes in a context-dependent manner, whereas T-bet expression did not confer a unique advantage in canonical in vitro suppression of Th1 proliferation. Together, these findings identify T-bet Tregs as a contact-capable regulatory subset embedded within early Th1-DC networks during the priming phase of type 1 inflammation rather than a destabilized or effector-converted Treg population.

papers.title: The immunogenic 33-mer gliadin peptide attenuates flagellin-induced TLR5/NF-κB signaling
papers.abstract: Wheat gluten is the main trigger of gluten-related disorders such as celiac disease, in which the proteolysis-resistant, 33-mer peptide is a key immunodominant factor. It has been reported that the 33-mer forms oligomers and thin-plate superstructures that accumulate in the Caco-2 intestinal epithelial cell line, although their biological effects remain only partially understood. Here, we screened the effects of these nanostructures on Toll-like receptors in Caco-2 cells to investigate their effect on the early innate immune response. Our findings showed a specific upregulation of TLR5 mRNA in response to 33-mer gliadin superstructures, although no inflammatory response was detected based on CXCL1 and CXCL8 levels. Moreover, immunofluorescence analysis revealed partial co-localization with TLR5. We further found that the 33-mer superstructures attenuate flagellin-induced TLR5/NF{kappa}B signaling in reporter cells, similar to a blocking anti-hTLR5-IgA2 antibody. Molecular docking suggested that the 33-mer peptide occupies the concave region of TLR5 as well as 54% of the TLR5-TLR5 dimerization interface. The interference with the TLR5 dimerization domain could explain the experimental attenuation of flagellin-mediated TLR5 activation. Given that TLR5 contributes not only to inflammation but also to intestinal homeostasis, our findings suggest that the formation of 33-mer nanostructures upon its accumulation may increase the local concentration of 33-mer, interfering with TLR5-mediated mucosal immune responses. These findings provide a rationale for investigating the role of TLR5 and 33-mer aggregates in clinical samples from patients with celiac disease and other gluten-related disorders.

papers.title: Tissue-resident memory T cells are diminished in the Kaposi sarcoma tumor microenvironment of people living with HIV
papers.abstract: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a rare neoplasm and an AIDS-defining diagnosis in people living with HIV (PLWH). Although and chronic infection with Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) contributes to KS progression, the local immune mechanisms that are lost during tumor progression remain incompletely understood. Here, we systematically characterized global patterns in the KS tumor microenvironment (TME) in both PLWH and HIV-negative individuals. Spatial transcriptomics revealed distinct niches comprising of tumor cells, immune cells, and surrounding skin cells. Tumor regions expressed a characteristic endothelial-fibroblastic signature attributable to KS tumor cells (CD34, LYVE1, SCN9A), TME regions expressed marker genes for T cells, B cells and cancer-associated fibroblasts. Analysis of putative cell-cell interactions demonstrated that tumor cells preferentially interact with cells of the TME, including T cells, indicating an important role as hub of cellular communication in KS. Immunofluorescence imaging confirmed increased numbers of T cells, specifically tissue-resident memory T cells (TRM), in KS samples compared to healthy skin, accompanied by a pronounced upregulation of PD-1 expression that was predominantly localized to the TME. Notably, we identified HIV-associated alterations in the KS immune microenvironment: PLWH exhibited loss of CXCR3+ and IFN-gamma producing CD8+ TRM cells in the KS TME compared to HIV-negative patients, a finding consistent with impaired antitumor immunity. Together, our findings reveal HIV-associated disruption of functional anti-tumor immunity in the KS TME of PLWH. Increased PD-1 expression within T cells of the TME highlights potential therapeutic use of immune checkpoint inhibitors in KS.

papers.title: Fast receptor-antigen dissociation kinetics promote CAR-T cell tumor infiltration, functional fitness, and antitumor efficacy in solid tumors
papers.abstract: Background: CAR-T cells have shown limited efficacy against solid tumors, where they face two major challenges: restricted tumor infiltration and sustained intensive engagement that drive them to exhaustion. Conventional CAR design has largely emphasized high-affinity interactions with slow dissociation, further limiting tumor infiltration and exacerbating exhaustion and dysfunction. We hypothesize that most current CARs are kinetically over-stabilized for solid tumors and that a fast-on/fast-off, cheek-kiss mode of engagement permits transient CAR-antigen disengagement, thereby facilitating tumor infiltration and preserving CAR-T cell fitness in tumor mass. Methods: We identified two monoclonal antibodies targeting the same epitope of epidermal growth factor receptor with comparable kon but distinct koff rates: cetuximab (Cet) and its humanized derivative H1. CAR-T cells incorporating these binders were evaluated in vitro and in vivo. Large, established human tumor xenografts were treated with low-dose CAR-T cells in NSG mice to model conditions of limited T cell availability and sustained tumor antigen exposure. Results: Cet and H1 exhibited comparable kon but markedly different koff rates, with H1 displaying fast-off kinetics with approximately 18-fold shorter binding dwell time. As CARs, H1 showed reduced antigen occupancy and less stable tumor-T cell engagement than Cet. Despite comparable in vitro cytotoxicity, H1 CAR-T cells accumulated more efficiently following tumor stimulation. At high doses, both CAR-T cell products eradicated established tumors. Under low-dose conditions, however, H1 CAR-T cells exhibited superior expansion, persistence, tumor infiltration, and antitumor efficacy, whereas Cet CAR-T cells showed limited expansion and only transient tumor control. Cet CAR-T cells progressively downregulated surface CAR expression, increased PD-1 expression, and exhibited reduced tumor infiltration and impaired functional recovery. In contrast, H1 CAR-T cells preserved surface CAR expression, exhibited greater tumor infiltration, maintained a less exhausted, more central memory-like phenotype, and retained effector function. Conclusion: Fast-on/fast-off binding kinetics enhance CAR-T tumor infiltration, expansion, persistence, and functional fitness, resulting in improved control of established solid tumors. The data provides a rationale for shifting CAR design from affinity optimization toward kinetic optimization to improve the efficacy and safety of CAR-T therapy for solid tumors.

papers.title: Spatial Transcriptomics Reveals Region-Specific Host Responses in Amoebic Gill Disease of Atlantic Salmon
papers.abstract: Amoebic gill disease (AGD), caused by the parasite Neoparamoeba perurans, is a major welfare and economic burden for the Atlantic salmon aquaculture industry. However, the spatial organisation of immune functions within the gill, the site of infection, remains poorly resolved. Here, we present the first spatial transcriptomic atlas of the Atlantic salmon gill affected by AGD, generated using 10x Genomics Visium on four AGD-positive fish, confirmed by gill scoring and quantitative PCR for parasite load. As no uninfected gills were included, this study maps the anatomical and immunological organisation of AGD-affected gills rather than defining AGD-specific pathology. Unsupervised clustering of spatial gene expression resolved distinct transcriptional domains that grouped into four principal anatomical compartments of the gill, including (i) epithelial and lamellar regions defined by keratin and osmoregulatory gene expression, (ii) gill arch regions enriched for connective tissue and smooth muscle markers, (iii) an erythroid-associated vascular cluster, and (iv) a skeletal muscle cluster with signatures of glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation. Across these domains, we identified a spatially organised and diffused immune landscape, with pattern recognition receptors, antimicrobial effectors and chemokines concentrated at the filament surface, and immunoglobulin light chain transcripts consistent with B lymphocyte activity enriched toward the gill arch. Integration of the spatial data with a published single-nucleus reference atlas using reference-based deconvolution resolved the cellular identity underlying these domains and revealed frequent co-localisation of immune and structural cell types, suggesting regulated cell to cell communication within the gill-associated lymphoid tissue. Overall, our results show that the Atlantic salmon gill is not a transcriptionally uniform surface but a regionally specialised organ, with immune functions distributed across, and specialised within, distinct anatomical compartments

papers.title: CXCR3 on transferred T cells enables vaccine-boosted adoptive T-cell therapy in solid tumors
papers.abstract: Adoptive T-cell therapy (ACT) has demonstrated marked clinical benefit in hematological malignancies but has limited efficacy against solid tumors. Cancer vaccines can improve ACT, but the mechanisms underlying this combination are poorly understood. Here, we combined ACT with chimpanzee adenovirus ChAdOx1 (ChAd) and modified vaccinia Ankara (MVA) encoding tumor antigens. Whereas PD1 blockade failed to improve ACT, the combination with ChAd/MVA vaccination drove durable regression of established tumors, correlating with expansion of tumor-reactive T cells in lymphoid organs and increased tumor infiltration by T cells. Mechanistically, ChAd priming induced CXCR3 ligands (CXCL10 and CXCL9) in the vaccine-draining lymph node, thereby recruiting transferred T cells to this node independently of cognate antigen. CXCR3 expression on the transferred T cells, but not on host cells, was required for the anti-tumor effect of the combination therapy and favored T-cell accumulation in the vaccine-draining lymph node and the tumor. These findings identify CXCR3 on the transferred T cells as a determinant of ACT plus vaccination synergy and provide a rationale for combining viral-vector vaccines with TCR-T therapies, and for selecting or engineering T cells to retain CXCR3 expression.

papers.title: Gut bacterium of Leishmania donovani-non-transmitting sand fly induces IL-23~Th17 axis to protect hosts from drug-resistant visceral leishmaniasis
papers.abstract: Background: Visceral leishmaniasis (VL) is caused by Leishmania donovani and differentiates under the influence of biotope-specific gut bacteria in the Leishmania donovani-transmitting sand fly vector, Phlebotomus argentipes, which coexists with the Leishmania donovani-non-transmitting Sergentomyia species in the Indian subcontinent. Hypothesis: Sergentomyia are primarily herpetophilic. Interestingly, we identified a specific population of anthropophilic Sergentomyia babu babu, a proven naturally non-competent vector for transmitting Leishmania donovani, with high abundance and human-bite incidences in VL-non-endemic regions, compared with VL-endemic regions of India. Thus, the possibility of egesting gut bacteria to humans from VL-non-transmitting Sergentomyia and inducing downstream immune cascades remains undeniable. Innovation: We characterized gut bacteria from anthropophilic Sergentomyia babu babu in both VL-endemic and VL-non-endemic regions of India and found that a heat-inactivated formulation of Heyndrickxia sporothermodurans [NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA): PRJNA1403236], isolated from anthropophilic Sergentomyia babu babu from a VL-non-endemic region, prevented and cured L. donovani infection by inducing IL-23~Th17. More importantly, it also prevented the initial parasite establishment by inducing phagocytosis, ROS, and TNF- in circulatory Ly6G-CD11b+Ly6Chi monocytes. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report confirming that the gut bacteria of VL-non-transmitting sand flies are critical and need to be investigated in depth for developing therapeutics and/or prophylactics against visceral leishmaniasis (VL), and suggests that possible bite-transfer of gut bacteria from disease-non-transmitting vectors to hosts may restrict disease pathogenicity. Further clinical trials are needed to warrant (Indian patent: 202511041013, April 28, 2025).

papers.title: Intracellular complement Factor B couples inflammatory sensing to metabolism, chromatin regulation and maladaptive tissue repair
papers.abstract: Inflammatory signals are broadly conserved, yet how tissue context converts them into programs of recovery or maladaptive repair remains unclear. Using kidney injury as a model of inflammation-to-repair transitions, we identify an injury-induced proximal-tubule complement program in which cell-intrinsic complement proteins are repurposed across subcellular compartments to couple inflammation to metabolic and chromatin regulation and promote maladaptive fibrotic remodeling. Mechanistically, myeloid-derived IL-1b; signals through IL-1R1 on injured tubular cells to recruit NF-kB and AP-1 to C3 and Cfb, coordinately inducing complement component 3 (C3) and Factor B (FB). Cytoplasmic FB drives cleavage-activation of cell-intrinsic C3, which supports tubular cell mitochondrial metabolic adaptation to stress and accumulation of C3aR-expressing macrophages around injured tubules. Nuclear FB, on the other hand, binds chromatin through a previously unrecognized DNA-binding interface and mediates histone H3 proteolysis and the preferential remodeling of chromatin promotors enriched in transcriptional programs relevant to maladaptive repair. Key features of this injury-associated C3-FB response, including intranuclear FB, are conserved in human kidney disease, associate with kidney dysfunction, and distinguish diseased from healthy kidneys. Together, these findings suggest that extracellular complement-targeting therapies may miss disease-relevant intracellular functions and suggest nuclear FB as a distinct target whose chromatin interaction and processing capacity could selectively limit maladaptive tissue responses beyond conventional inhibition.

papers.title: Robust V(D)J Recombination in the Absence of SA1/2-mediated Chromatin Loops
papers.abstract: The cohesin ring complex organizes and mediates functional activity of the genome through chromatin loop extrusion1,2. Cohesin comprises a core SMC1-SMC3-RAD21 ring associated with multiple regulatory proteins, including SA1 and SA2 paralogs that bind mutually-exclusively to a RAD21 site3,4. Functional studies of cohesin complexes in vivo often employ inactivation of particular components2,3. However, inactivation of SA1 or SA2 in mice is limited by mouse embryonic lethality5-7 and, for dual SA1/2-inactivation by cycling cell lethality8-10. For these reasons, it remains unknown whether the requirement for SA1/2 in loop extrusion in vitro11,12 applies in vivo1,2, and whether these factors have overlapping or distinct functions in regulating this process3. Here, we employ G0/G1-arrested v-Abl pro-B lines, which are viable in the absence of cohesin-complex factors13,14, to dissect SA1 and SA2 functions in V(D)J recombination, a strictly G0/G1-specific process that harnesses loop extrusion to effect distinct Igh and Ig{kappa} locus recombination mechanisms15,16. Robust long-range Igh or Ig{kappa} V(D)J recombination continued unabated in the absence of SA1 or SA2. However, inactivation of both abrogated most positioned chromatin loops genome-wide and also abolished long-range Igh V(D)J recombination with a phenotype similar to RAD21 (cohesin) inactivation13. Yet, robust Ig{kappa} V(D)J recombination continued upon dual SA1/2-inactivation, which along with Hi-C findings, demonstrates ongoing loop-extrusion in the absence of SA1/2. Correspondingly, replacement of weak Igh V(D)J recombination signal sequences (RSSs) that target V(D)J recombination activity, with strong Ig{kappa} counterparts15 restored long-range Igh V(D)J recombination in SA1/2 inactivated cells. We conclude that SA1/2 together maintain loop extrusion impediments and genome-wide architecture in G0/G1-arrested cells; and, in their absence, loop extrusion proceeds unimpeded. Remarkably, strong RSSs allow Ig{kappa} to function normally in the absence of internal positioned loop structure across the 3.1-mega-base Ig{kappa} locus. We discuss implications of our findings for long-range gene regulation in G0/G1-arrested cells more broadly.

papers.title: CD19 CAR Engineered T Regulatory Cells Promote Durable Immune Tolerance in Experimental Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
papers.abstract: While the immune reset induced by CD19 CAR T therapies has shown striking promise in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), the nature and duration of benefit mediated by B cell depletion remains unclear. Loss of tolerance in SLE is driven by extrafollicular and germinal center interactions between dendritic cells and self-reactive T and B cells. We hypothesized that CD19 CAR-engineered regulatory T cells (CAR19 EngTreg), capable of suppressing multiple autoimmune effector cell types, might promote long-term tolerance without producing high-levels of inflammatory mediators. To generate CAR19 EngTreg, we combined CD19 CAR delivery with homology directed repair at the FOXP3 locus to drive constitutive, stable FOXP3 expression in CD4 T cells. CAR19 EngTreg expressed canonical Treg markers; exhibited minimal inflammatory cytokine production; and blocked human B cell differentiation into antibody secreting plasma cells. In humanized mouse models, transfer of CAR19 EngTreg led to a reduction in B cell numbers with low inflammatory cytokine production relative to CD19 CAR Teff, and reduced tissue inflammation. In a short-term, in vivo imiquimod-induced inflammatory model, murine CAR19 EngTreg reduced skin pathology, spleen size, and inflammatory cytokines. Finally, in two distinct mouse models of lupus, CAR19 EngTreg persisted for >4 months leading to reduced autoimmune T and B effector populations, sustained reduction in multiple autoantibodies and improved renal function and histopathology. Thus, CAR19 EngTreg may offer a promising and durable therapeutic avenue for B cell-mediated autoimmune disorders capable of long-term regulation of both autoreactive B and T cells.

papers.title: Tissue retention of dendritic cells drives age-associated protective tolerogenic lymphoid structures
papers.abstract: Ectopic lymphoid structures are typically associated with chronic tissue inflammation in autoimmunity and cancer, where they can amplify local immune responses. Similar structures arise spontaneously with age, yet their origin and function remain unclear. Here we identify tissue retention of mature migratory conventional dendritic cells (cDCs) as a driver of age-associated lymphoid organization. Mature cDCs accumulated within lymphoid structures in aged human and mouse tissues. We demonstrate that impaired cDC egress or pharmacological cDC expansion induced de novo structures in mice across multiple otherwise homeostatic organs without associated pathology. Strikingly, senescence-associated tissue cues, which promoted a distinct cDC maturation state, were required for lymphoid niche initiation. Unlike inflammatory structures described in disease, these cDC-driven structures preferentially accumulated tissue-adapted regulatory T cells and protected against inflammatory injury, revealing a previously unrecognized regulatory dimension of age-associated lymphoid organization.

papers.title: The Mitochondria-Modulating Small Molecule TEM1657 Suppresses NFKBIZ Pathway and Resolves Th17-Driven Psoriatic Inflammation
papers.abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic skin disease characterized by red, scaly plaques mainly driven by dysregulated T cells that induce keratinocytes (KCs) proliferation and inflammation. Despite significant advancements in disease management through biologics and topical therapies, these treatments offer only temporary relief and fail to prevent disease recurrence. Considering the current therapeutic needs, we described herein a novel small molecule TEM1657, derived from 3,5-dicaffeoylquinic acid with anti-inflammatory potency in imiquimod-induced psoriasis mouse model as well as in Th17-stimulated KCs. Mechanistically, its action is mediated through modulation of mitochondrial dynamics, specifically via OPA1, an inner mitochondrial membrane protein that alters mitochondrial calcium influx, and further impacts cellular bioenergetics. Moreover, TEM1657 rapidly suppresses transcription of NFKBIZ and various other psoriasis-associated genes. These observations highlighted a pathway that represents an innovative target in psoriasis and other NFKBIZ-related disorders.

papers.title: Archaeal cell envelopes selectively activate innate immunity through TLR2 in contrasts with multi-receptor bacterial sensing
papers.abstract: The cell envelope of bacteria and fungi is a major source of microbial-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs), which are recognised by multiple host pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) such as TLRs and NODs. The key role of this recognition in protecting against infection and regulating diverse physiological processes has been studied for decades. In contrast, although the archaea are growingly recognised as an important component of the animal and human microbiome, their interaction with the innate immune system has been largely understudied. Here, we asked whether the archaeal cell envelope acts as MAMP. We selected 15 archaeal species from different environments, including the human microbiome, and harbouring diverse envelope characteristics, and we tested their ability to activate innate immune responses in human and murine immune cells. We first show that archaeal cells activate the innate immune transcription factor NF-kB and induce IL-6 secretion. Using whole archaeal cells, supernatants, and purified envelope components, we then find that none of the main PRR receptors which recognise the bacterial envelope (TLR4, TLR5, NOD1 and NOD2) are involved in this activation. We only detected activation of TLR2, regardless of the environmental origins of the archaea tested, although with overall lower activity compared to bacteria. We further demonstrate that different TLR2 heterodimers are involved, depending on the species, although the archaeal agonist remains unknown. Altogether, our results highlight a surprising paucity of interaction of archaeal cell envelope components with host PPRs, in contrast to bacteria, and open new avenues of research toward further investigation of archaea/host interplay.

papers.title: A semi-automated tool for improving Assessments and Lab Tests data annotation in ImmPort
papers.abstract: Public data sharing in immunological and clinical research is essential for transparency, reproducibility, and secondary analysis. However, many datasets in repositories such as ImmPort lack sufficient structured data to enable reuse. ImmPort's Assessments and Lab Tests templates -- which capture critical clinical information -- are often incomplete or omitted due to their complexity and the manual effort required. To address this challenge, an application with a graphical user interface requiring no programming was developed to facilitate population of these templates. The tool streamlines the submission process by reducing time and complexity for data contributors while ensuring template formatting. It integrates ImmPort files, study-specific data files, and a curated data dictionary to automate the mapping of study variables to the required fields within each template. The tool was evaluated on seven ImmPort studies with diverse designs. It successfully generated submission-ready templates that passed ImmPort's internal validation and will be incorporated into the repository. By improving the feasibility and completeness of templates, this approach enhances the quality, findability, and reusability of data within ImmPort.
